Hp.definition: Pressure altitude: altitude in the ISA atmosphere corresponding to the entered static pressure.
Hp.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. Geometric altitude is converted before the atmosphere calculation.
Hp.physics: Hydrostatic balance relates pressure to altitude in the layered ISA atmosphere. Inverting that pressure profile gives an equivalent pressure altitude, not a measurement of height above the ground.

Hg.definition: Geometric altitude: physical height above mean sea level.
Hg.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. Geometric altitude is converted before the atmosphere calculation.
Hg.physics: Geometric height measures distance above sea level. The spherical-Earth conversion accounts for weakening gravity when converting between geometric and geopotential altitude.

P.definition: Static atmospheric pressure. AeroCalculator converts it to pressure altitude.
P.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. Geometric altitude is converted before the atmosphere calculation.
P.physics: The ISA hydrostatic pressure profile represents the weight of the air column above the selected level. Local density then follows the ideal-gas relation using the entered temperature.

Δ ISA.definition: Temperature deviation from the ISA temperature at the current pressure altitude.
Δ ISA.physics: The temperature offset changes the local thermal state at the same pressure altitude. Warmer air at fixed pressure has lower density; colder air has higher density.

OAT.definition: Outside air temperature at the aircraft condition.
OAT.physics: Static air temperature sets density and sound speed. Adding the ISA temperature offset gives the local temperature without changing the selected pressure level.

TAS.definition: True Airspeed: aircraft speed relative to the surrounding air mass.
TAS.physics: True airspeed measures motion through the air mass. Combining it with local density sets dynamic pressure; combining it with local sound speed gives Mach number.

CAS.definition: Indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position errors. CAS is related to impact pressure using standard sea-level references.
CAS.physics: CAS is the speed in standard sea-level air that produces the same pitot impact pressure. The subsonic isentropic conversion accounts for compression as the flow is brought to rest.

EAS.definition: Equivalent Airspeed: speed at standard sea-level density with the same dynamic pressure as the current flight condition.
EAS.physics: EAS preserves dynamic pressure when replacing the actual density with standard sea-level density. Equal EAS gives equal aerodynamic force for the same area and lift coefficient.

Mach.definition: Mach number: True Airspeed divided by the local speed of sound.
Mach.limits: 0 ≤ M < 1 for the current compressibility model.
Mach.physics: Mach compares airspeed with the speed of pressure disturbances in the local air. The pitot conversion used here describes subsonic, isentropic deceleration with gamma = 1.4.

CL.definition: Lift coefficient. With mass, load factor and reference area, it defines the required dynamic pressure.
CL.physics: The lift equation balances aerodynamic lift against the selected normal load, n times weight. Increasing mass or load factor requires more dynamic pressure or a larger lift coefficient.

Vs Factor.definition: Multiplier applied to the 1-g calibrated stall speed. The optional +Δ term is added in knots.
Vs Factor.physics: The multiplier scales the 1-g stall reference expressed as CAS; the optional delta adds a fixed speed in knots. It specifies a speed margin and does not by itself prescribe a maneuver load factor.

Ground Speed.definition: Aircraft speed relative to the ground. Wind and direction inputs are used to recover the air-relative velocity.
Ground Speed.physics: The ground-velocity vector is the sum of air-relative velocity and wind velocity. Directions and sideslip determine the vector components; scalar speeds cannot simply be added for arbitrary wind angles.

Qdyn.physics: Dynamic pressure is kinetic energy per unit volume of moving air. It scales aerodynamic forces and rises with density and the square of true airspeed.

Qc.definition: Impact pressure qc = total pressure minus static pressure for the documented subsonic model.
Qc.physics: A pitot opening brings the flow to rest and converts kinetic energy into compression. Impact pressure is stagnation minus static pressure; it approaches dynamic pressure at low Mach number.

Weight.definition: Aircraft mass used for lift, stall-speed and maneuver calculations.
Weight.physics: The entered quantity is mass; multiplying by standard gravity gives weight. The selected normal load factor then sets the lift required by the maneuver.

Sref.definition: Wing reference area used in aerodynamic force and coefficient calculations.
Sref.physics: Reference area is the chosen normalization area in the lift equation. A larger area produces more lift at the same dynamic pressure and lift coefficient; it does not determine wing shape.

cref.definition: Wing reference chord used to calculate Reynolds number.
cref.physics: Reference chord sets the length scale for Reynolds number. Comparing inertial transport with molecular viscosity at that scale characterizes the flow regime; this calculation does not predict transition or separation.

CLmax.definition: Maximum lift coefficient used to calculate the 1-g stall speed.
CLmax.physics: The limiting lift coefficient sets the lowest 1-g speed that can support the aircraft weight. Its value must come from aircraft data for the chosen flap configuration; the calculator does not predict it from geometry.

NzPullup.definition: Normal load factor for a pull-up maneuver. Bank angle is zero.
NzPullup.physics: Normal load factor is lift divided by weight. The unbanked pull-up model increases lift demand without introducing the bank relation used for a level turn.

NzTurn.definition: Normal load factor in a coordinated level turn. Bank angle is derived from Nz = 1/cos(φ).
NzTurn.physics: In a coordinated level turn, the vertical component of lift balances weight and the horizontal component provides centripetal acceleration. This gives n = 1/cos(bank), with bank magnitude below 90 degrees.

BankTurn.definition: Bank angle for a coordinated level turn. Load factor is derived from Nz = 1/cos(φ).
BankTurn.physics: In a coordinated level turn, the vertical component of lift balances weight and the horizontal component provides centripetal acceleration. This gives n = 1/cos(bank), with bank magnitude below 90 degrees.

Track.definition: Track angle: direction of the ground-velocity vector.
Track.physics: Track is the direction of the ground-velocity vector. Wind shifts it away from the air-relative direction through the horizontal wind triangle.

Heading.definition: Heading angle: direction the aircraft longitudinal axis points.
Heading.physics: Heading describes the aircraft longitudinal axis. Sideslip relates that axis to the air-relative velocity, and wind then determines the ground track.

Sideslip.definition: Sideslip angle β: angle between the aircraft heading and the air-relative velocity direction.
Sideslip.physics: Sideslip is the angular difference between the aircraft axis and its air-relative motion. The wind triangle uses it to orient the airspeed vector; it does not calculate side force or yaw dynamics.

Drift.physics: Drift is heading minus ground track. It combines the effects of wind and the selected sideslip rather than describing a force or an aerodynamic coefficient.

HeadWind.definition: Wind component along the selected runway/reference direction. Positive means headwind.
HeadWind.physics: Projecting wind onto the selected runway axis gives the headwind component. A positive value opposes motion along that axis; a negative value is tailwind.

Wind Speed.definition: Wind-vector magnitude. Use Wind Direction for its direction.
Wind Speed.physics: Wind speed is the magnitude of the horizontal wind vector. Resolving or combining its perpendicular components preserves that vector magnitude.

CrossWind.definition: Wind component perpendicular to the selected runway/reference direction.
CrossWind.physics: Projecting wind onto the axis perpendicular to the runway gives the signed crosswind component. Together with headwind it reconstructs the horizontal wind vector.

Runway Angle.definition: Reference direction used to resolve headwind and crosswind components.
Runway Angle.physics: The runway/reference direction defines the axes for headwind and crosswind. Rotating those axes changes the components without changing the physical wind vector.

Wind Direction.definition: Direction from which the wind is referenced in the wind-vector input mode.
Wind Direction.physics: Wind direction follows the meteorological convention: the direction the wind comes from. The velocity vector points the opposite way; zero wind has no physical direction.

mass.MTOW.definition: Maximum mass approved for takeoff for the selected aircraft configuration. The value is supplied by the aircraft profile.
mass.MTOW.use: Reference mass for takeoff-condition calculations when selected.
mass.MTOW.physics: This aircraft-data mass describes the selected takeoff loading limit. It enters the force balance as weight through m times standard gravity; the calculator does not derive the approved limit.

mass.MLW.definition: Maximum mass approved for landing for the selected aircraft configuration. The value is supplied by the aircraft profile.
mass.MLW.use: Reference mass for landing-condition calculations when selected.
mass.MLW.physics: This aircraft-data mass describes the selected landing loading limit. It enters lift and stall calculations through weight; the calculator does not derive the approved limit.

mass.MZFW.definition: Maximum aircraft mass without usable fuel, as defined by the aircraft data. The value is supplied by the aircraft profile.
mass.MZFW.use: Reference mass for zero-fuel-mass calculations when selected.
mass.MZFW.physics: Zero-fuel mass separates the aircraft and payload loading from usable fuel. The stored value supplies mass to the force balance rather than being inferred from wing geometry.

mass.BOW.definition: Basic operating mass as defined by the aircraft operator or aircraft data. The value is supplied by the aircraft profile.
mass.BOW.use: Stored reference mass for calculations that use the selected aircraft mass.
mass.BOW.physics: Basic operating mass represents the equipped aircraft baseline defined by its operator. Selecting it supplies a mass for the lift and stall-speed equations.

mass.Heavy.definition: User-defined heavy reference mass for the selected aircraft. This label has no standardized regulatory definition.
mass.Heavy.use: User-defined reference mass for calculations that use the selected aircraft mass.
mass.Heavy.physics: This user-defined reference mass specifies a loading case. It supplies weight to the aerodynamic force balance; the label does not impose a universal aircraft limit.

mass.Light.definition: User-defined light reference mass for the selected aircraft. This label has no standardized regulatory definition.
mass.Light.use: User-defined reference mass for calculations that use the selected aircraft mass.
mass.Light.physics: This user-defined reference mass specifies a loading case. It supplies weight to the aerodynamic force balance; the label does not impose a universal aircraft limit.

CLmaxFlap.full: Maximum lift coefficient by flap setting
CLmaxFlap.definition: Maximum lift coefficient recorded for one aircraft flap configuration. Each value is supplied by the aircraft profile.
CLmaxFlap.use: Used with mass, density, and reference area to calculate reference stall speed.
CLmaxFlap.physics: The limiting lift coefficient sets the lowest 1-g speed that can support the aircraft weight. Its value must come from aircraft data for the chosen flap configuration; the calculator does not predict it from geometry.

Pressure Altitude.definition: Pressure altitude: altitude in the ISA atmosphere corresponding to the entered static pressure.
Pressure Altitude.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. See the documented geometric-altitude temperature convention.
Pressure Altitude.physics: Hydrostatic balance relates pressure to altitude in the layered ISA atmosphere. Inverting that pressure profile gives an equivalent pressure altitude, not a measurement of height above the ground.

Geometric Altitude.physics: Geometric height measures distance above sea level. The spherical-Earth conversion accounts for weakening gravity when converting between geometric and geopotential altitude.

Lift Coefficient CL.limits: Available when dynamic pressure and reference area are positive. The sign follows the selected load factor.
Lift Coefficient CL.physics: The lift equation balances aerodynamic lift against the selected normal load, n times weight. Increasing mass or load factor requires more dynamic pressure or a larger lift coefficient.

Heading Angle Ψ.physics: Heading describes the aircraft longitudinal axis. Sideslip relates that axis to the air-relative velocity, and wind then determines the ground track.

Drift Angle.physics: Drift is heading minus ground track. It combines the effects of wind and the selected sideslip rather than describing a force or an aerodynamic coefficient.

Sideslip Angle β.physics: Sideslip is the angular difference between the aircraft axis and its air-relative motion. The wind triangle uses it to orient the airspeed vector; it does not calculate side force or yaw dynamics.

Vs Factor.physics: The multiplier scales the 1-g stall reference expressed as CAS; the optional delta adds a fixed speed in knots. It specifies a speed margin and does not by itself prescribe a maneuver load factor.

Mach.definition: Mach number: True Airspeed divided by the local speed of sound.
Mach.limits: 0 ≤ M < 1 for the current compressibility model.
Mach.physics: Mach compares airspeed with the speed of pressure disturbances in the local air. The pitot conversion used here describes subsonic, isentropic deceleration with gamma = 1.4.

Wind Speed.physics: Wind speed is the magnitude of the horizontal wind vector. Resolving or combining its perpendicular components preserves that vector magnitude.

Wind Direction.definition: Direction from which the wind is referenced in the wind-vector input mode.
Wind Direction.physics: Wind direction follows the meteorological convention: the direction the wind comes from. The velocity vector points the opposite way; zero wind has no physical direction.

Geopotential Altitude.definition: Effective gravitational altitude used by the standard atmosphere.
Geopotential Altitude.equation: H = r h / (r + h); for Hp/P input, H = Hp − 29.271247 ΔT ln(p/p0)
Geopotential Altitude.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. See the documented geometric-altitude temperature convention.
Geopotential Altitude.physics: Geopotential height expresses gravitational potential as an equivalent height at standard gravity. For pressure-altitude input, the temperature correction represents the changed thickness of a warmer or colder air column.

Density Altitude.definition: ISA altitude with the same density as the current condition.
Density Altitude.physics: Density altitude is the ISA level with the same air density as the current condition. It summarizes density effects on aerodynamic forces without claiming that the aircraft is physically at that height.

Temperature Altitude.definition: Altitude returned by the documented temperature-altitude convention. Temperature alone is not a unique altitude across all layers.
Temperature Altitude.physics: This is a tropospheric temperature-equivalent height, using the ISA lapse rate. Temperatures at or below 216.65 K return 11 km in this convention; temperature alone cannot identify a unique altitude across all ISA layers.

Density.definition: Mass of air per unit volume.
Density.physics: The ideal-gas equation links density to static pressure and absolute temperature for dry air. At the same pressure, heating expands the air and reduces its mass per unit volume.

Total Temperature.definition: Isentropic stagnation temperature for a calorically perfect gas.
Total Temperature.physics: Adiabatic deceleration converts kinetic energy into internal energy, raising temperature as the air is brought to rest. The ideal stagnation relation uses a constant specific-heat ratio of 1.4, without a probe recovery correction.

Viscosity.definition: Dynamic viscosity from the documented temperature correlation.
Viscosity.physics: Sutherland correlation represents the temperature dependence of molecular momentum transport in air. Dynamic viscosity increases with temperature and supplies the viscous scale in Reynolds number.

Sound Speed.definition: Local speed of sound in the ideal-gas model.
Sound Speed.physics: Small pressure disturbances propagate through ideal air at a speed set by absolute temperature and the specific-heat ratio. Warmer air has a higher sound speed.

Stall Speed Vs.definition: 1-g reference stall speed displayed as CAS, independent of maneuver load factor.
Stall Speed Vs.equation: Vs,TAS = √(2 m g0 / (ρ S CLmax)); displayed Vs,CAS = CAS(Vs,TAS)
Stall Speed Vs.physics: At the 1-g stall reference, maximum lift just balances weight. The result is converted from TAS to CAS; maneuver load factor does not alter this reference value.

Reynolds.definition: Ratio of inertial and viscous effects based on reference chord.
Reynolds.physics: Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous effects over the reference chord. Increasing speed, density, or chord increases this ratio; increasing viscosity reduces it.

Pressure Ratio δ.definition: Pressure divided by standard sea-level pressure.
Pressure Ratio δ.physics: Dividing static pressure by standard sea-level pressure gives a dimensionless atmospheric pressure scale. It is used to normalize weight and compare conditions across pressure levels.

Density Ratio σ.definition: Density divided by standard sea-level density.
Density Ratio σ.physics: The density ratio compares local air density with standard sea-level density. Its square root relates true and equivalent airspeed at equal dynamic pressure.

Temperature Ratio θ.definition: Absolute temperature divided by standard sea-level temperature.
Temperature Ratio θ.physics: The temperature ratio compares absolute local temperature with the standard sea-level temperature. Absolute temperature is required because molecular thermal energy sets sound speed and the ideal-gas density relation.

Total Pressure.definition: Stagnation pressure from the subsonic isentropic relation.
Total Pressure.physics: Stagnation pressure is the pressure after ideal subsonic, isentropic deceleration to rest. Adding pitot impact pressure to static pressure gives this total pressure; shocks and flow losses are not modeled.

DynPressure * S / g.definition: Dynamic pressure times reference area, expressed as force in kgf.
DynPressure * S / g.physics: Dynamic pressure times reference area gives an aerodynamic force scale before multiplying by a force coefficient. Dividing by standard gravity expresses that force in kgf; it is not aircraft mass.

Lift Force.definition: Lift required by the selected mass and maneuver, displayed in kgf.
Lift Force.equation: L / g0 = q S CL / g0 (displayed as kgf)
Lift Force.physics: Lift is dynamic pressure times reference area and lift coefficient, and equals the selected normal load times weight. The displayed kgf value converts that force using standard gravity.

Weight/Delta W/δ.definition: Weight normalized by pressure ratio, displayed in kgf.
Weight/Delta W/δ.physics: Dividing weight by pressure ratio normalizes the aircraft load to standard sea-level pressure. The kgf display is a force normalization, not a change in the actual aircraft mass.

Load Factor Nz.definition: Selected normal load factor. In a coordinated level turn, the load factor follows the selected bank angle or determines the bank angle.
Load Factor Nz.physics: Normal load factor measures lift relative to weight. In the level-turn mode it follows the vertical lift balance; in pull-up mode it is supplied directly.

Turn Radius.definition: Signed level-turn radius, unavailable at zero bank.
Turn Radius.physics: The horizontal component of lift supplies centripetal acceleration in a coordinated level turn. More bank tightens the turn at a fixed TAS; zero bank gives no finite turn radius.

Turn Rate.definition: Signed angular turn rate under the level-turn assumption.
Turn Rate.physics: Turn rate is the angular response to the centripetal acceleration supplied by banked lift. At a fixed bank, increasing TAS reduces the rate; the sign follows the selected turn direction.

AlongTrack Headwind.definition: Positive headwind opposes travel along the calculated track.
AlongTrack Headwind.physics: Projecting wind against the calculated ground track gives the along-track headwind. Positive headwind reduces the ground-speed component relative to motion through the air.

AlongTrack Crosswind.definition: Signed crosswind component in the documented convention.
AlongTrack Crosswind.physics: Projecting wind perpendicular to the calculated ground track gives its signed lateral component. This is a change of reference axes, not an additional wind velocity.
